subject: Structured covariance estimation with ragged arrays - feedback requested

messages.author: f5e508a8c6c4988c
messages.subject: Structured covariance estimation with ragged arrays - feedback requested
parts:
Hi,

I recently ran into a situation that suggested a "clustered" or vector regression model such that:
  1. The dimension of the random vector varies from cluster to cluster,
  2. The covariance matrices of the residuals are structured and depend on a fixed number of parameters.
In existing software, I couldn't find any options that would allow for this, so I turned to Stan. I created a simple simulation in R where there is a structured covariance matrix for the vector (X1, X2, X3) such that:
  • Var(X1) = Var(X2) = sigma_a^2,
  • Var(X3) = sigma_b^2,
  • Cov(X1, X2) = rho1,
  • Cov(X1, X3) = rho2,
  • Cov(X2, X3) = rho2,
Where the clustered observations are observed as one of: (X1, X2), (X1, X3), (X2, X3), or (X1, X2, X3).

In my Stan code, I believe I got it to work by creating a "master" covariance matrix in transformed parameters and then putting sub-segments of the data vector into local variable of fixed size in the model block. The only bad thing is having to "repeat myself" for every vector size:

  for (i in 1:n_clusters) {
    p = subj_upper[i] - subj_lower[i] + 1;
    if (p == 2) {
      mu_2 = rep_vector(0, 2);
      Sigma_2 = Sigma[type[subj_lower[i]:subj_upper[i]],
                      type[subj_lower[i]:subj_upper[i]]];
      y_vec2 = to_vector(y[subj_lower[i]:subj_upper[i]]);
      y_vec2 ~ multi_normal(mu_2, Sigma_2);
    } else if (p == 3) {
      mu_3 = rep_vector(0, 3);
      Sigma_3 = Sigma[type[subj_lower[i]:subj_upper[i]],
                      type[subj_lower[i]:subj_upper[i]]];

      y_vec3 = to_vector(y[subj_lower[i]:subj_upper[i]]);
      y_vec3 ~ multi_normal(mu_3, Sigma_3);
    }
  }

Also, as an inexperienced bayesian practitioner, there are a few additional points that concern me:
  • My priors don't ensure positive definiteness,
  • Stan gives a warning message about my "transformation" of the data into the cluster-sized variables,
  • There seems to be some bias in the posterior draws, but perhaps this is expected
Hopefully this example is interesting to the group. I'm looking for general feedback and better ways to implement this type of model.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Structured covariance estimation with ragged arrays - feedback requested
parts:
On Sunday, December 18, 2016 at 12:27:51 PM UTC-5, Ben Ogorek wrote:
In my Stan code, I believe I got it to work by creating a "master" covariance matrix in transformed parameters and then putting sub-segments of the data vector into local variable of fixed size in the model block. The only bad thing is having to "repeat myself" for every vector size:
It would probably be better to pass the data as two (or n_clusters) vectors, one for each cluster.

Also, as an inexperienced bayesian practitioner, there are a few additional points that concern me:
  • My priors don't ensure positive definiteness,

Then your priors do not integrate to 1 over admissible region of the parameter space. To be positive definite, you need to declare rho2 as

real<lower=-bound(rho1),upper=bound(rho1)> rho2;

where bound is defined in the functions block as

real bound(real rho1) return sqrt( 1 / ( 1 + (1 - rho1) / (1 + rho1) ) );
• Stan gives a warning message about my "transformation" of the data into the cluster-sized variables,
That is an identity "transformation" and thus the Jacobian matrix is the identity matrix, whose log-determinant is a constant (zero), so no adjustment needs to be made.
• There seems to be some bias in the posterior draws, but perhaps this is expected

from the lack of positive definiteness.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Structured covariance estimation with ragged arrays - feedback requested
parts:
Hi Ben,

Thanks for this helpful information. I did not realize I was incurring bias by putting prior mass on impossible outcomes.

In reviewing my matrix algebra, I see that for this simple 3x3 case, it's possible to derive simple algebraic relationships between rho1 and rho2 that ensure positive definiteness. One way seems to be to ensure the determinant of the entire 3x3 correlation matrix is itself positive.

Of course, when I scale up to a larger matrix for my real life situation (a sports problem), I'm probably not going to be able to derive simple bounds like this with, say, 5 different correlations in a 12x12 matrix. It looks like there's some literature out there discussing similar issues (like this paper), but I'd be interested in hearing if there are other tricks Stan users have in the face of complex constraints.

messages.author: f5e508a8c6c4988c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Structured covariance estimation with ragged arrays - feedback requested
parts:
I'm helping a friend with a fantasy football game where players choose a "lineup" of 1 Quarterback (QB), 3 Wide Recievers (WR), 2 Running Backs (RB), a Tight End (TE), a "Flex player" (WR, RB, or TE), and a defense. Points are awarded at the player level based on performance in a single game, and thus these picks can be from the same team or different teams. But within-team player correlations are part of the strategy; if a QB has a high "scoring" game, then the WRs from the same team are also more likely to have high scoring games.

My approach seeks to incorporate these player correlations by modeling the weekly match-up vectors between teams. These will be of variable dimension, but one match-up vector might look like:

(QB, WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4, RB1, RB2, RB3, TE1, TE2, Def)

I'd like to structure the correlation matrix such that:
  * Corr(QB,  WRj) = rho_qb_wr
  * Corr(QB,  RBj) = rho_qb_rb
  * Corr(QB,  TEj) = rho_qb_te
  * Corr(QB,  Def) = rho_qb_def
  * Corr(WRi, WRj) = rho_wr, i /= j
  * Corr(RBi, WRj) = rho_rb_wr
  * Corr(WRi, TEj) = rho_wr_te
  * Corr(WRi, Def) = rho_wr_def
  * Corr(RBi, RBj) = rho_rb, i /= j
  * Corr(RBi, TEj) = rho_rb_te
  * Corr(RBi, Def) = rho_rb_def
  * Corr(TEi, TEj) = rho_te, i /= j
  * Corr(TEi, Def) = rho_te_def

If my math is right, that's 110 possible correlations down to 13. But will the problem of getting reasonable priors for the rho's be tractable?

Additionally, since this is a covariance matrix modeling problem, I also considered the structural equation model:

QB_points ~ sum(WR_points) + sum(RB_points) + ... + Def_points,
WR1_points ~ sum(WR_not_WR1_points) + sum(RB_points) + ... + Def_points,
...

This would induce a player correlation matrix, but I dropped it when I considered what a pain it would be to simulate from.

messages.author: f5e508a8c6c4988c
messages.subject: Re: Structured covariance estimation with ragged arrays - feedback requested
parts:
One final wrap-up post on this topic:
  • I added Ben G's bounding function to the original stan file where the data is in long format.
  • Another of Ben's suggestions was separate the 2 and 3 dimensional vectors in R before passing them into Stan. As can be seen here, the model block is much cleaner.
  • Finally, this last stan file goes after the covariance parameters indirectly, via latent variable modeling. Aside from the looping (which I know is making things slow), I think this is the way to go; extending Ben's correlation bounds to higher dimensions apparently involves solving for roots of higher order polynomials.
The driver program for the previous file is still a single R program.

It's probably too late to help my friend with his fantasy football game, but I learned a lot about bayesian modeling and Stan. Thanks for the help and advice!

Ben Ogorek
